docs.D01_business_overview.md:
Title: Global payment networks — transaction infrastructure, not card lenders
Source: compiled from: https://s29.q4cdn.com/385744025/files/doc_downloads/2025/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf; https://s25.q4cdn.com/479285134/files/doc_financials/2025/ar/MA-12-31-2025-10-K-as-filed-with-standard-exhibits.pdf
Date: 2026-02-11

Visa and Mastercard connect consumers, issuing banks, merchants, acquiring institutions and processors. Their networks authorize, route, clear and support settlement of payments, while related services include security, authentication, analytics and other capabilities. They are not ordinarily the institutions lending revolving balances to cardholders.

This distinction matters economically. A card interest-rate cap directly affects lenders' revenue and underwriting, while routing mandates or network-fee competition can affect network economics more directly. Interchange, merchant discount, issuer interest and the networks' own fees are not the same revenue stream.

The moat is multi-sided acceptance. Consumers value broad merchant acceptance; merchants value access to paying customers; banks and processors value reliable global connectivity, fraud controls and established standards. Replacing one technical message is easier than replicating the full ecosystem, customer protections and commercial relationships.

Scale can support high incremental margins because processing another transaction does not require proportional physical investment. Nevertheless, technology, cybersecurity, incentives, sales relationships and regulatory compliance are ongoing costs. Client incentives are significant and affect reported net revenue.

Visa's FY2025 net revenue was $40.000 billion and operating income $23.994 billion. Mastercard's calendar-2025 revenue was $32.791 billion and operating income $18.897 billion. Different fiscal calendars, litigation provisions and service mix limit simple margin comparisons.

The growth base includes nominal consumer spending, digitization of cash payments, e-commerce, cross-border travel/commerce and services sold around the payment relationship. Cross-border activity often has different economics from domestic transactions, so total transaction growth alone does not settle revenue growth.

Ryan McInerney leads Visa and Michael Miebach leads Mastercard. Both companies are investing in tokenization, identity and AI-enabled commerce. The existence of those programs shows adaptation, not proof that new rails cannot threaten existing economics.

Stablecoins can offer alternative settlement, especially for some cross-border and business use cases. AI shopping agents may influence which payment method is selected. The underwriting issue is whether trusted credentials, acceptance, fraud protection, recourse and issuer relationships preserve network value as interfaces change.

Owning both businesses would diversify company-specific execution but retain common exposure to consumer spending, regulation, network pricing and technological substitution. They should therefore be treated as related holdings rather than independent sources of portfolio diversification.
docs.D02_financial_snapshot.md:
Title: Three-year network earnings and cash conversion
Source: compiled from: https://s29.q4cdn.com/385744025/files/doc_downloads/2025/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf; https://s25.q4cdn.com/479285134/files/doc_financials/2025/ar/MA-12-31-2025-10-K-as-filed-with-standard-exhibits.pdf
Date: 2026-02-11

Dollar figures are millions except EPS. Visa years end September 30; Mastercard years end December 31. FCF below is calculated using explicitly stated investment lines, not assumed to be each company's identically defined non-GAAP measure.

| Metric | Visa 2023 | Visa 2024 | Visa 2025 | MA 2023 | MA 2024 | MA 2025 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Net revenue | 32,653 | 35,926 | 40,000 | 25,098 | 28,167 | 32,791 |
| Operating income | 21,000 | 23,595 | 23,994 | 14,008 | 15,582 | 18,897 |
| Diluted EPS | 8.28 | 9.73 | 10.20 | 11.83 | 13.89 | 16.52 |
| CFO | 20,755 | 19,950 | 23,059 | 11,980 | 14,780 | 17,648 |
| Physical/technology capex | 1,059 | 1,257 | 1,482 | 371 | 474 | 489 |
| Separately capitalized software | Included above | Included above | Included above | 717 | 720 | 726 |
| CFO less both investment lines | 19,696 | 18,693 | 21,577 | 10,892 | 13,586 | 16,433 |
| Cash-flow repurchases | 12,101 | 16,713 | 18,316 | 9,032 | 10,954 | 11,727 |
| Dividends | 3,751 | 4,217 | 4,634 | 2,158 | 2,448 | 2,756 |

Visa's calculated FY2025 operating margin was 60.0%, versus 65.7% in 2024. Litigation provision increased from $462 million to $2.562 billion. That affects GAAP growth and should not be mistaken for equivalent deterioration in underlying transaction economics.

Mastercard's FY2025 calculated margin was 57.6% versus 55.3%. Its reported EPS rose despite a higher tax expense. Comparisons of adjusted margins require company-specific reconciliations rather than removing only whichever costs are inconvenient.

Visa's latest January release reports $16.9 billion cash/equivalents/investment securities and $19.602 billion long-term debt. Mastercard's year-end cash was $10.566 billion, with $749 million short-term and $18.251 billion long-term debt. These definitions exclude some settlement/restricted assets and do not represent identical liquidity classifications.

Latest-quarter Visa revenue was $10.9 billion, GAAP EPS $3.03 and adjusted EPS $3.17. Mastercard Q4 revenue was $8.8 billion, GAAP EPS $4.52 and adjusted EPS $4.76. Strong cash conversion is observable; a consistent ROIC series and exact normalized earnings bridge are not included.
docs.D03_latest_results_and_guidance.md:
Title: January results — spending, cross-border activity and services
Source: compiled from: https://s1.q4cdn.com/050606653/files/doc_financials/2026/q1/Q1-2026-Earnings-Release_vF.pdf; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1141391/000114139126000003/ma12312025-exx991xearnings.htm
Date: 2026-01-29

Both networks reported results January 29, but their periods differ. Visa reported fiscal Q1 2026; Mastercard reported Q4 and calendar 2025. The information is current before this March cutoff, not evidence about later spring spending.

Visa net revenue was approximately $10.9 billion, up 15% reported and 13% constant dollar. GAAP net income was approximately $5.9 billion, GAAP EPS $3.03 and non-GAAP EPS $3.17. Payments volume increased 8% constant dollar, total cross-border volume 12% and processed transactions 9%.

Cross-border totals can include intra-Europe activity; they should not automatically be treated as the higher-yielding ex-intra-Europe measure. The provided summary uses the total metric explicitly. Revenue growth above payments-volume growth reflects mix, pricing, services and timing, not necessarily a change in every transaction's fee.

Visa reports 1.93 billion diluted weighted-average Class A equivalent shares. That is a weighted-average conversion-based denominator rather than exact March outstanding shares. The company continues substantial shareholder distributions, but a complete current-quarter cash-flow bridge is not reproduced here.

Mastercard Q4 revenue was approximately $8.8 billion. GAAP net income was $4.1 billion, EPS $4.52 and adjusted EPS $4.76. Gross dollar volume rose 7% local currency, cross-border volume 14% and switched transactions 10%.

Mastercard value-added services and solutions revenue rose 26% reported and 22% currency-neutral. That is a disclosed growth rate, not an August portfolio manager's later estimate of services mix. The exact contribution to incremental operating profit requires additional segment reconciliation.

Full-year Mastercard revenue grew 16% reported and 15% currency-neutral. Both companies' latest data therefore show growing payments activity and monetization rather than an observed collapse in usage. These results precede any later AI-related disruption evidence.

Exact next-quarter/full-year guidance from the accompanying calls and a verified March consensus estimate were not recovered. The pack deliberately does not substitute later results or a later investor's forward multiple for missing guidance. An analyst must model spending, cross-border mix, pricing, incentives, services and capital return explicitly.

The key forward test is whether current cash generation remains durable as payment interfaces evolve. Strong January results support the starting earnings base but cannot alone disprove long-run fee compression or displacement.
docs.D04_price_and_valuation.md:
Title: March 31 valuation — separate denominators, common uncertainty
Source: compiled from: https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/V/history/?period1=1774915200&period2=1775001600; https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/MA/history/?period1=1774915200&period2=1775001600; https://s1.q4cdn.com/050606653/files/doc_financials/2026/q1/Q1-2026-Earnings-Release_vF.pdf; https://s25.q4cdn.com/479285134/files/doc_financials/2025/ar/MA-12-31-2025-10-K-as-filed-with-standard-exhibits.pdf
Date: 2026-03-31

Visa closed March 31 at $302.24 on 10,246,900 shares. The session range was $296.59–303.34. Mastercard closed $499.66 on 4,417,600 shares, with range $490.58–501.41. These are unadjusted historical closes rather than later price widgets.

Visa's Q1 diluted weighted-average Class A equivalent shares were 1.93 billion. Multiplication gives a calculated diluted equity-value proxy of $583.323 billion. Mastercard's Q4 diluted weighted-average 898 million shares gives $448.695 billion. Neither is an exact cutoff market capitalization.

Using Visa's latest $16.9 billion cash/investment balance and $19.602 billion long-term debt gives a simple EV proxy around $586.025 billion before other adjustments. Using Mastercard's year-end $19.0 billion total debt and $10.566 billion cash gives approximately $457.129 billion EV. Settlement/restricted funds and other liability treatments matter.

| Calculated historical valuation | Visa | Mastercard |
|---|---:|---:|
| Prior-year reported EPS | $10.20 | $16.52 |
| Price / that EPS | 29.6x | 30.2x |
| Prior-year CFO less stated capex/software | $21.577bn | $16.433bn |
| Yield on equity-value proxy | 3.7% | 3.7% |
| EV / prior-year operating income | 24.4x | 24.2x |

Visa's GAAP EPS includes a large litigation provision, so the historical P/E differs from a normalized or adjusted comparison. Mastercard's software capitalization is deducted explicitly in the cash residual; omitting it would overstate comparative cash yield.

The last row is operating income, not EBITDA. An authenticated cutoff consensus forward EPS series, exact EV/EBITDA, current 52-week ranges, historical own-forward-multiple distributions and same-date S&P 500 forward P/E are missing.

An authenticated March31 forward ratio requires the matching earnings forecast, not merely a quoted price. A forward investment case must show the forecast that produces its ratio and allow for policy/technology effects on fees.

The observed trading volumes suggest substantial liquidity, but buying both names doubles exposure to a related economic thesis. Liquidity and business quality should not obscure the need for correlated downside scenarios and separate position sizing.
docs.D05_market_worries.md:
Title: Agents, stablecoins and proposed credit-card regulation
Source: compiled from: https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-07/stablecoin-firms-bet-big-on-ai-agent-payments-that-barely-exist; https://finance.yahoo.com/news/visa-mastercard-arent-real-casualties-133113889.html; https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/stock-market-cpi-today-inflation-01-13-2026/card/visa-mastercard-shares-drop-after-trump-endorses-credit-card-bill-4TxzQPadSUn1ibPQhOEa; https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/3623/text
Date: 2026-03-07

Emily Mason's March 7 Bloomberg report describes stablecoin firms building for AI-agent payments and notes that a Citrini scenario about agents bypassing card fees shook card-network shares two weeks earlier. This is a dated description of market concern, not proof that mass agentic bypass already occurs.

Kaustubh Bagalkote's February 28 Benzinga account emphasizes that Citrini's “2028 Global Intelligence Crisis” was explicitly “a scenario, not a prediction.” Its mechanism is nevertheless analytically relevant: agents might select cheaper settlement rails, weakening consumer inertia and network pricing.

The bear case must distinguish consumer-facing convenience from the underlying payment stack. If agents can cheaply acquire identity, authorization, risk allocation and merchant acceptance elsewhere, card tolls could compress. If they still need trusted credentials, issuer credit and consumer recourse, the networks may remain important infrastructure.

Regulation is a separate risk. Xavier Martinez's January 13 Wall Street Journal account reports shares falling after Trump endorsed the Credit Card Competition Act; Visa fell 4.5% that session. Congress's primary text shows S.3623 introduced January 13, proposing rules on competition in credit-card transaction networks.

The proposal is not assumed enacted, defeated or permanently stalled at this cutoff. Routing competition could pressure network economics differently from a proposed cap on card interest. A cap primarily affects lenders, with possible indirect effects on credit availability and spending; the networks do not ordinarily earn cardholder interest.

Stablecoins could address real pain points in cross-border transfers and business settlement. Those markets are not identical to consumer credit-card purchases with rewards, dispute resolution and fraud protection. Adoption in one use case does not prove immediate replacement in every other use case.

Counterevidence includes January transaction growth, high cash conversion and announced network investment in AI/tokenization. But management programs are responses to risk, not independent proof the moat is invulnerable.

The serious question is the earnings sensitivity to lower take rates, alternate routing and changing checkout behavior. Recession, travel mix, client incentives, litigation and cybersecurity also remain risks. Current fear should be quantified against the actual profit pool rather than either extrapolated to total collapse or dismissed because current earnings are strong.
docs.D06_peer_and_industry_benchmarks.md:
Title: Distinguishing networks, lenders and digital wallets
Source: compiled from: https://fortune.com/company-assets/1678/quartr/earnings-release-8-k-d61e2-2026-01-30-12-23-01.pdf; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1633917/000163391726000021/pypl4q-25earningsrelease.htm; https://s25.q4cdn.com/479285134/files/doc_financials/2025/ar/MA-12-31-2025-10-K-as-filed-with-standard-exhibits.pdf; https://s29.q4cdn.com/385744025/files/doc_downloads/2025/Visa-Fiscal-2025-Annual-Report.pdf
Date: 2026-02-11

Visa and Mastercard are each other's closest listed global network comparison. American Express and PayPal are useful adjacent benchmarks but have different business models. Treating all payment companies as one homogeneous sector would confuse credit risk, merchant acquisition, network fees and wallet/checkout economics.

American Express's January 30 release reports 2025 net income of $10.8 billion and EPS $15.38. Worldwide billed business was approximately $1.670 trillion. Its integrated model combines network, merchant relationships and cardholder lending, so an interest-rate cap can affect it differently from a non-lending network.

PayPal's February 3 release reports Q4 transaction-margin dollars of $4.034 billion versus $3.935 billion, up 3%, or $3.741 billion excluding interest on customer balances, up 4%. This is a non-GAAP operating metric, not net revenue or operating income. Customer-balance interest and checkout economics distinguish it from the networks.

| Calendar/fiscal 2025 observation | Visa | Mastercard |
|---|---:|---:|
| Revenue | $40.000bn | $32.791bn |
| Operating margin, calculated | 60.0% | 57.6% |
| CFO less stated capital investment | $21.577bn | $16.433bn |
| Latest reported cross-border growth | 12% total | 14% |

The cross-border figures come from different latest quarters and definitions; they are not a perfectly synchronized market-share comparison. Visa's operating margin includes substantial litigation provision, so adjusted economics require reconciliation.

Both networks have high cash conversion and broad acceptance. Their common advantage is a trusted multi-party system rather than simply the visible card logo. Their shared risk is that regulation or alternative rails reduce the fee pool faster than volume and services can expand it.

Digital wallets may use existing card rails rather than replace them. Stablecoin settlement may similarly complement some parts of the stack while competing with others. The key is tracing which participant retains authorization, settlement, identity, credit, fraud and customer-service economics.

Exact cutoff peer forward multiples, harmonized capital returns and comparable FCF yields are unavailable. No unsupported ranking is supplied. The operating evidence instead helps separate genuinely different payment profit pools and identify which bear mechanism applies to each.
docs.D07_event_timeline.md:
Title: Technology initiatives and the first-quarter fear cycle
Source: compiled from: https://usa.visa.com/about-visa/newsroom/press-releases.releaseId.21366.html; https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/3623/text; https://s1.q4cdn.com/050606653/files/doc_financials/2026/q1/Q1-2026-Earnings-Release_vF.pdf; https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1141391/000114139126000003/ma12312025-exx991xearnings.htm; https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-07/stablecoin-firms-bet-big-on-ai-agent-payments-that-barely-exist
Date: 2026-03-31

April 30, 2025: Visa publicly announced AI-commerce initiatives opening its network to AI platforms, technology firms, banks, fintechs and merchants. This is pre-cutoff evidence that the company was developing agent-compatible capabilities, not a later announcement moved backward into March.

During 2025: Stablecoins and alternative payment rails attracted growing interest. Their potential use in settlement and cross-border transfers is distinct from proof of universal consumer-card replacement. This document does not assign an exact adoption rate without a dated source.

December 2025: Visa's annual report made its fiscal 2025 financials available, including $40 billion revenue and a large litigation provision. Mastercard's February 2026 10-K later supplied its calendar-year statements. Different reporting calendars are preserved in D02.

January 13, 2026: The Credit Card Competition Act of 2026 was introduced. Contemporary market reporting linked network-stock declines to Trump's endorsement. Its legal status at this point is a proposal, not completed network-fee reform.

January 29: Both networks reported growing transactions and cross-border activity. Visa fiscal Q1 revenue rose 15% reported; Mastercard Q4 services growth was 26% reported. These are the latest included company results.

February: A hypothetical AI-disruption scenario described agents avoiding card fees. Subsequent reporting says it contributed to share-price pressure. The scenario is not a report of already-observed mass displacement and should not be labeled a forecast certainty.

March 7: Bloomberg described stablecoin providers racing to build agent-payment systems, while emphasizing how early the use case remained. That captures the tension between a plausible new infrastructure market and limited current operating evidence.

March 31: Visa closed $302.24 and Mastercard $499.66. The snapshot ends before any unpinned second-quarter transaction window. No later earnings, regulatory conclusion or investor explanation is included.

The live question is whether technological change removes the networks' economic role, shifts it or enlarges it. A responsible model must make the affected revenue and margin assumptions explicit, not equate all digital payment innovation with either inevitable disruption or guaranteed incremental growth.
docs.D08_pershing_context.md:
Title: A related pair of franchises within a concentrated capital base
Source: compiled from: https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/11144917/2026-Annual-Investor-Presentation.pdf; https://assets.pershingsquareholdings.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/15162701/PSH-Fact-Sheet-December-2025-Website.pdf
Date: 2026-02-11

The February 11 presentation reports February 9 gross core-fund AUM of $19.748 billion and core equity $16.077 billion. PSH gross assets were $17.872 billion and equity $14.202 billion. Gross assets include financing and are not identical to available cash.

The presentation's December 31 capital weights include Amazon 13%, Meta 10% and Hertz 2%. Other publicly discussed franchises include Alphabet, Brookfield, Uber, Universal Music, Restaurant Brands, Howard Hughes and Fannie/Freddie exposure. Exact March weights and cash were not independently reconstructed.

The December fact sheet describes a concentrated strategy, generally eight to twelve core large-cap liquid North American businesses, with one to three new core investments annually. A full US reportable-stock table would not capture every foreign, OTC or derivative exposure and should not be treated as a complete NAV allocation.

Public investment principles emphasize simple, predictable FCF, durable competitive barriers, strong finances, capable management and limited dependence on capital markets or extrinsic factors. Visa and Mastercard should be tested against those standards through actual transaction economics, not because the word “network” resembles other successful holdings.

The two companies offer a potential fit with recurring, capital-efficient toll economics. Yet their earnings are not contractual annuities: spending, travel, regulation, incentives and technology can change. Buying both would require a combined exposure limit because much of the downside narrative is shared.

The portfolio already has substantial technology-enabled franchise exposure. Card networks might diversify product-market demand, but could also add another position sensitive to AI-related valuation and consumer spending. Correlation must be assessed economically rather than by sector labels alone.

No verified pre-March-31 Visa/Mastercard-specific Ackman recommendation is included. The analysis is therefore a fresh application of public principles to the evidence, not an imitation of an unpublished investment explanation.

Exact entry sizing cannot be inferred from the manager's overall AUM. Each candidate requires its own downside case, prospective return and liquidity plan, followed by a joint check on shared regulation and rail-displacement risk. Permanent capital permits patience but does not justify capitalizing uncertain fee growth as if it were guaranteed.

drivers.driver: Dense global acceptance networks support capital-light transaction tolls without ordinary lender credit exposure.
Cash displacement, e-commerce, nominal spending and faster-growing services support compounding.
Agentic commerce and stablecoins need not bypass trusted authorization, recourse and acceptance; networks can integrate the new technology.
Regulatory and disruption fears created an attractive roughly22x forward entry valuation.
drivers.quote: among the highest-quality businesses in the world

answer_key.pack_quality_notes: 8 joint documents, separate three-year fiscal calendars/cash tables and precise historical closes. Pre-Q2 March31 cutoff avoids unpinned entry-day hindsight. Forward consensus, exact historical/52week ranges and peer forward valuations missing. Latest call guidance not recovered. August services-mix and regulatory-stalling claims excluded from March documents. Joint key does not assume identical sizes or executions.

valuation.downside_case: P/E contraction to 18-20x and growth deceleration due to legislative and technological headwinds

drivers.driver: A dominant, capital-light global payment duopoly with significant network effects and durable secular growth tailwinds [D01].
We were able to acquire our stake at ~30x earnings, a fair price for a high-quality franchise capable of double-digit compounding [D04].
Management teams are proactively investing in AI, tokenization, and identity services to secure long-term network relevance [D01, D07].
The earnings algorithm is driven by secular cash digitization, e-commerce growth, cross-border activity, and disciplined share buybacks [D01, D02, D03].

The market fears that regulatory legislation and new payment technologies will erode the duopoly, but these threats are overstated as the networks provide essential security, trust, and global interoperability [D05, D07].

kill_criteria: Successful legislative passage and enforcement of the Credit Card Competition Act that materially caps swipe fees or mandates routing competition, permanently impairing margins.
Two consecutive quarters of deceleration in cross-border or total transaction volume growth indicating a loss of network ubiquity.
Evidence that AI-agents or stablecoin-based settlement protocols are achieving meaningful market share capture of core merchant-consumer transactions, bypassing the card rails.
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A fundamental, structural impairment of the network economics through either permanent legislative fee caps or the successful large-scale displacement of card rails by decentralized payment protocols.
final.memo:
The Company and the Companystercard operate the world's most important global payment networks, facilitating the movement of money through secure, multi-sided ecosystems [D01]. These businesses represent our ideal standard: they are simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative, and possess a dominant moat built on deep network effects that provide essential trust and interoperability to merchants and consumers worldwide [D01].

Currently, the market is mispricing these franchises due to misplaced fears regarding the Credit Card Competition Act and the emergence of alternative payment technologies like AI-agents and stablecoins [D05, D07]. We believe these concerns are overstated, as the networks are already aggressively deploying tokenization and identity services to ensure their infrastructure remains the bedrock of future global payments [D01, D07].

We were able to acquire our stake at approximately 30x prior-year earnings, a valuation that we view as highly attractive for businesses of this quality [D04]. Given the secular tailwinds in cash digitization, e-commerce, and cross-border volume, we expect the companies to deliver double-digit EPS growth over the next five years, supplemented by consistent share repurchases [D01, D02, D03].

Our role is one of patient, long-term capital support as the market eventually looks past the current regulatory and technological noise [D01, D03]. As execution continues and the resilience of these models is proven, we anticipate a natural rerate that will compound our capital at an attractive internal rate of return [D03, D04].

Our primary risk remains that sustained legislative or technological intervention forces a material degradation of the networks' unit economics [D05, D07]. We will closely monitor volume growth and the evolution of the competitive landscape to ensure our thesis holds [D03, D05].

We are initiating a 10% position in the companies, reflecting our high conviction in their long-term compounding potential and their status as essential global financial utilities [D08].

valuation.eps_path: 12% CAGR based on historical volume and services growth
valuation.downside_case: Legislative capping of interchange fees forces a step-down in network economics, leading to a permanent re-rating of the terminal multiple to 15-18x and stunted EPS growth.

drivers.driver: Visa and Mastercard operate as a dominant, capital-light global payment duopoly with significant competitive moats and highly scalable infrastructure [D01, D02].
The market has incorrectly priced these franchises due to temporary fears regarding the Credit Card Competition Act and AI-driven disintermediation [D05, D07].
The core businesses continue to exhibit durable growth, with January 2026 reports confirming robust transaction volumes and cross-border strength [D03, D07].
Operating margins remain sector-leading at 57-60%, providing strong free cash flow to support share repurchases and dividends [D02].
These companies act as essential, high-trust global infrastructure that is not easily replaced, securing their long-term position in digital commerce [D01].

kill_criteria: Legislative enactment of the Credit Card Competition Act that effectively caps interchange fees and reduces the networks' take rates [D05].
A measurable shift in consumer and merchant preference toward alternative, non-card settlement rails that bypass the duopoly's infrastructure [D05].
A persistent decline in transaction volume growth over two consecutive quarters, signaling a fundamental loss of network relevance [D03].
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A fundamental degradation of network economics caused by permanent legislative price controls or a verifiable loss of market share to disruptive alternative settlement technologies.
final.memo:
Visa and Mastercard represent the type of simple, predictable, and free-cash-flow-generative franchises that form the core of our Pershing Square 3.0 strategy [D01, D08]. These companies function as the essential, high-trust global infrastructure for electronic payments, benefiting from profound multi-sided network effects that create significant barriers to entry [D01]. With operating margins exceeding 57% and a capital-light business model, they consistently produce durable growth through the digitization of cash, e-commerce, and value-added services [D01, D02, D03].

The current opportunity exists because of a temporary market dislocation caused by the introduction of the Credit Card Competition Act on January 13, 2026, and speculative fears regarding AI-driven disintermediation [D05, D07]. We believe these concerns are fundamentally misplaced, as the market fails to distinguish between regulatory headlines and the persistent underlying utility of these payment networks [D01, D05]. Recent performance data from January 2026 underscores our view, showing 7-8% volume growth despite the heightened regulatory noise [D03, D07].

We are acquiring our position at an NTM multiple of approximately 30x, which we view as attractive for a compounder capable of delivering double-digit EPS growth [D03, D04]. Assuming a 12% CAGR, we model a compelling IRR of roughly 21% based on a terminal multiple of 25x [D03, D04]. While we acknowledge the risk of legislative interference, our base case assumes that the fundamental economics of the duopoly will remain intact [D01, D05].

Our role is that of a long-term owner of a quality compounder, providing the patience required for the market to reconcile the intrinsic value of these franchises with their current trading price [D08]. We remain vigilant regarding the regulatory landscape and the evolution of alternative payment rails, but we do not anticipate needing to intervene in the management of these dominant businesses [D01, D05]. We will monitor these factors closely to ensure our thesis regarding their durable competitive advantage remains sound [D05].

We are establishing a target position size of 10% of our NAV, reflecting our high conviction in the long-term compounding potential of these networks [D08]. This position is liquid, allowing us to build our stake over the coming weeks without adverse market impact [D01, D02]. By investing at this point of dislocation, we position our portfolio to benefit from the continued digitization of the global economy through these unique, high-moat assets [D01, D08].
